                 COMMENTS OF CENTERPOINT ENERGY HOUSTON ELECTRIC, LLC

         CenterPoint Energy Houston Electric, LLC (“CenterPoint Energy” or the “Company”)

                                  Proposed Rule 25.192 Amendments

A.       Use of 12CP

service. CenterPoint Energy supports using this methodology for se ng the TSP rate for

transmission service.1 As stated in the Company’s Project No. 58484 comments, the ERCOT grid

has evolved beyond a tradi onal summer-peaking system. Recently, winter monthly peaks have

 C.     ERCOT Adjustments to DSP 12CP Load Values

       Subsec on (f)(1)(B) of the 25.192 proposed amendments requires ERCOT to adjust the

DSP 12CP load values of each DSP that has an interconnected, transmission-level large load

D.     Interim Update Adjustment for ADFIT

changes in transmission-related accumulated deferred federal income taxes.” The Company

rate proceeding, so that the process aligns with an approved change in the Company’s cost of

service baseline. Further, the proposed ADFIT adjustment encompasses upda ng ADFIT amounts

that pertain to transmission plant currently not included in interim rate updates, crea ng a

mismatch where the underlying ADFIT is included but the investment that generated that ADFIT

is not included. Therefore, the Company recommends that if a requirement to adjust ADFIT as

                              Proposed Rule 25.193 Amendments

A.     Annual Update of Class Alloca on Factor Values

       CenterPoint Energy supports the requirement that DSPs update class alloca on factor

values annually. Annual updates reduce the lag and cost misalignment that occur when alloca on

factors remain sta c between comprehensive base rate proceedings.

B.     The Large Load Minimum Billing Demand Should Transi on to an NCP Floor When the
       Twenty-Year Period Ends

       Proposed 25.193(d)(2) sets the large load minimum billing demand at the greater of

contracted peak demand, prior-year non-coincident peak ("NCP") demand, or 12CP demand, and

proposed 25.193(d)(3) requires that billing con nue for at least twenty years. Because contracted

peak demand stays in the greater-of calcula on and will usually be the largest of the three, the

prac cal eﬀect is a bill fixed at the full contracted level for two decades, whatever the customer

actually does. CenterPoint Energy supports that framework. A firm commitment term, a

contracted ramp schedule, financial security posted at execu on, and payments beginning when

capacity is made available are all sound.


       The problem is what happens when the twenty years run out. Other customers are

protected for as long as the customer exists up to 20 years under the current framework. Financial

security covers the early years, and the minimum billing demand covers years one through

twenty. Nothing covers year twenty-one. On that date the customer is free to curtail during

coincident peak intervals while con nuing to rely on transmission facili es built and sized for its

 full demand. Those facili es do not go away, and neither do their costs. They shi to residen al

and other retail classes, all at once, at the end of a period during which no one was required to

think about them. As proposed, the rule reduces and defers the cost-shi ing ques on rather than

solving it.


           The Company therefore recommends a two-phase approach. During the contracted ramp-

up period, billing should occur as proposed, based on capacity made available under the

customer's ramp schedule and regardless of whether the customer has energized. Once the

       An NCP-based backstop charges large loads on the basis of their actual maximum use of

the system, which is the measure used to size transmission infrastructure. A contracted-demand

floor charges them on the basis of a number wri en into an agreement years earlier. The backstop

aligns cost recovery with cost causa on and preserves the incen ve to reduce genuine NCP

demand, which is the reduc on that actually avoids future investment.


       The backstop is not puni ve, because a customer controls its own floor. A customer that

genuinely reduces its opera ons lowers its NCP and lowers its floor along with it, in the same

month. The provision reaches only a customer that maintains a high maximum demand while

concerned about, and it is the only behavior the provision addresses.

reduced load during an emergency would carry an inflated billing determinant for twelve months

G.   Proposed 25.193(f) Should not prohibit transmission costs recovery through the DSPs base rates

       Proposed 25.193(f) inexplicably strikes the language that allows an adjustment to a DSP’s TCRF

charges in a base rate proceeding. This would limit the DSP from recovering any cost through the

transmission function in base rates. As the transmission system evolves, it could be advantageous to

move a portion of the transmission costs back to base rates. This would provide an avenue to

moderate swings due to seasonality as the TCRF over / under grows.

                                  Proposed New Rule 25.252

A.     Applicability

       This proposed new rule imposes requirements on large load retail customers and the

investor-owned DSPs who have a duty to interconnect with and provide distribu on service to

them. This proposed new rule also purports to apply to “TSPs providing transmission service.”

See proposed rule subsec on (a). However, nothing in this proposed new rule is applicable to

transmission service and, therefore, nothing in it is applicable to TSPs, since TSPs only provide

transmission service. TSPs provide transmission service (or “wholesale transmission service” as

when the service is provided at transmission-voltage levels.13 A transmission and distribu on

u lity (“TDU”) is a DSP when it provides retail delivery services and a TSP when it provides

wholesale transmission services.

B.       Distribu on Interconnec on Costs and Transmission Interconnec on Costs Defini ons

Briefly, the terms “distribu on-level customer” and “transmission-level customer” used,

intended scope for this rule to apply only to interconnec ons of distribu on-level large load retail

customers and transmission-level large load retail customers, respec vely. The Company also

requests clarifica on on whether distribu on system upgrade costs and transmission system

1.       Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be

Values should not differ by contracted peak demand or NCP demand level. The relevant

§25.193(d)(2) sets the minimum billing demand as the greater of contracted peak demand,
highest NCP demand in the past year, or 12CP demand. Each is a per-customer measured or

Through NPRR1308 and NOGRR282, ERCOT established requirements applicable to Large

three years of events in which such loads tripped or instantly reduced consumption during system

The minimum billing demand exists because a capacity reservation may not be used as

2.       Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
         a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
         b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
         c. extended to a longer time period?
There are two logical ways to keep large load costs off other customers. The first is to have the
customer pay for its upgrades in cash up front, which takes those costs out of the shared pool
before anyone is billed. The second is to leave the costs in the pool and make the customer's
payment through the DSP to the TSP high enough to capture the cost of the capacity built for it.

     -   If the customer pays for its upgrades in full, those costs are already out of the shared pool.
         A minimum billing demand is still needed during the ramp-up period, so a customer
         cannot hold capacity while paying nothing toward it. After that, the better tool is a
         backstop based on the customer's actual peak demand.
     -   If the customer pays nothing up front, which is what the rule provides today for a
         customer that performs, the costs stay in the pool and the minimum billing demand
         backed by a financial security is the only thing keeping them off other customers.

A minimum billing demand term and the Company's proposed NCP backstop are not competing
ideas. The two instruments address different populations. The minimum billing demand protects
against the customerthat failsto coverall of its costs, leaving capacity built and unused and costs
for others to carry. A non-coincident peak backstop addresses a different risk: the customer that

                                                   19
 succeeds, remains on the system past the minimum billing demand period, and then curtails
during coincident peak intervals to reduce its transmission charges. That customer has not failed
and has not left stranded costs behind, but the demand it places on the system has not changed,
and its avoided share shifts to customers with less ability to respond to peak signals.

The distinction matters because a long-tenured customer should not be penalized for efficiency,
if the capacity can be used by future customers. A customer that permanently reduces its load,
or operates more efficiently, is placing less demand on the system, and its transmission charges
should fall accordingly. A customer that maintains the same demand but shifts it around the
coincident peak intervals is not reducing what the system must be built to serve. An NCP-based
backstop distinguishes between the two, because it measures the customer's maximum demand
on the system rather than its demand during a handful of measured intervals. It preserves the
incentive to reduce load while preventing cost shifts from load that has merely become eligible
to be rescheduled.

CenterPoint Energy therefore recommends that the minimum billing demand and the NCP
backstop be understood as sequential rather than alternative. The minimum billing demand
governs the period during which capacity has been built and the customer's commitment is
unproven. The NCP backstop governsthereafter, forthe successful, long-tenured customer whose
cost responsibility should track the demand it actually places on the system.

3.        Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
          lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
           load minimum billing demand:
          a.            reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
                        is some percentage of the customer's contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
                        demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in
                        phases over the years, and how?
           b.           be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the large
                        load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
                        customer's contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
                        year and the large load customer's 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
                        weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
                        over the years, and how?
CenterPoint recommends alternative (a), a ratchet set as a percentage of the customer's
maximum NCP demand, with the percentage adjustable by the Commission. The Company does
not recommend that the percentage decline over time. Alternative (b) should not be adopted.

NCP demand is the customer's own highest demand. It is what transmission planners use to size
the facilities that serve the customer, so it is the closest available measure of what the customer
caused the system to build. Contracted peak demand, by contrast, reflects what the customer
asked for at the time it signed. Where the two differ, NCP is the better measure.

A percentage of maximum NCP also does something a fixed contract number cannot. It keeps a
large customer contributing on the basis of its own highest demand even when the customer
succeeds in avoiding the specific intervals used to allocate cost. This is the concern CenterPoint

                                                                      21
 raised in Project 58484. Large customers have the tools and the staff to shift load away from those
intervals. Residential customers and smaller commercial customers do not. When the large
customer avoids the interval, the cost does not disappear. It moves to the customers who could
not avoid it.

The Company recommends that the ratchet apply only when it is needed, rather than in every
month. In any month in which the customer's coincident peak demand falls below 70 percent of
its NCP demand for that same month, the coincident peak recorded for that month is set to that
month's NCP multiplied by the class coincident-to-non-coincident peak ratio from the prior year,
currently about 87 percent in CEHE. A customerthat stays within 30 percent of its own maximum
is billed on what it actually used. This is the same mechanic the Company describes above forthe
post-commitment backstop, and using one structure for both keeps a single large load
determinant in the rule rather than two.

The percentage should be adjustable, and that is the main advantage of alternative (a). It gives
the Commission one dial to turn as conditions change, without reopening the structure of the
rule.
The Company does not recommend that the percentage decline in phases. A declining percentage
withdraws protection from other customers on a schedule, without answering what happens
once it is gone. The transmission facilities serving these loads do not get cheaper over time, and
the customer's ability to avoid peak intervals does not fade.

Alternative (b) should not be adopted because it makes the floor move. A customer's 12CP
demand depends on when the system peaks and on what every othercustomerdoes duringthose
intervals. Building that into a minimum billing demand means the minimum itself changes for
reasons the customer did not cause and cannot predict. A floor that moves is not a floor. The
customer cannot forecast what it owes, and the utility cannot forecast what it will recover. There
is also no need to put 12CP into the minimum, because 12CP already sets the ordinary billing
determinant through the network transmission service rate, which CenterPoint recommends
continue elsewhere in these comments.

The Company's recommendation does not have this problem, and the difference is timing. The
ratchet looks at a coincident measure only after the fact, to decide whether the floor applies to a
month that has already ended. The multiplier comes from the prior year's completed data. Both
are known before the billing year starts. Alternative (b) puts a live coincident measure inside the
determinant itself, where no one can see it coming.

Finally, a weighted average is harder to administer and harder to explain to a customer than a
single percentage, and it offers no flexibility that a percentage ratchet does not already provide.

       entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection
       Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power
       electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and

       loads.
Yes, subject to two qualifications: what separate rate treatment should mean, and how the class
should be defined.

Separate treatment of the determinant, not a separate rate.

CenterPoint recommends that the minimum billing demand in §25.193(d), apply to Large
Computational Loads ratherthan to all large load customers. CenterPoint does not recommend a
separate rate class. The rate per kVA for service at a given voltage should continue to be the class
rate derived from the transmission revenue requirement and class billing determinants. The
billing determinants determined by the actual 12CP of "traditional customers" and the minimum
billing demand for large computational load customers.

A differentiated billing determinant assigns a customer a share of shared costs that reflects the
capacity built for it; the revenue requirement, the rate, and every other customer's rate are
untouched. A differentiated rate requires a class cost of service study allocating a distinct revenue
requirement to a new class, along with the record to support it. Nothing before the Commission
in this project supports the second. The first follows directly from the risk the minimum billing
demand exists to manage.

The transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study are those
transmission system upgrade projects needed to serve all of the load that was studied in the
batch study, not any particular load project, and not any of the base load customers that were
modeled but not studied in the batch study.
This question implies that the costs of transmission system upgrade as defined in the proposed
rule amendments in this Project are presently not intended to be included in the transmission
interconnection costs definition. As the Company stated in its comments, however, that is not

6.      If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether
       the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should
       these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and
       transmission planning studies?
The Company does not believe a large load customer is able to reserve for itself any capacity
created by system upgrades that were not covered by the customer's CIAC. No load customer
has the ability or right to reserve capacity on facilities that are dedicated to serve the public. The
Commission's own pro forma Tariff for Retail Delivery Service precludes a customer from
obtaining a guaranteed right to a particular level of capacity on a TDU's system. Sections 4.2.1
and 5.2.1 of that tariff provide, in pertinent part, as follows:
       Company will make reasonable provisions to supply steady and continuous
       Delivery Service but does not guarantee the Delivery Service against fluctuations
       or interruptions. Company will not be liable for any damages... occasioned by
       fluctuations or interruptions unless it be shown that Company has not made
       reasonable provision tosupplysteadyand continuous Delivery Service, consistent
       with the Retail Customer's class of service.
A reservation of capacity obligation on a TDU would render these tariff provisions all but
meaningless. Assuming that a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity, the
load level of the reserved capacity should be modeled at that level for a period of time that is
sufficient to develop an operational history of the load.          After that period passes, if it is
determined that the customer's historical load level is consistently below the amount of the
reserved capacity, then the customer's historical peak rather than its reserved capacity should be
used, at least in transmission planning studies.
